clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in HCN1, which encodes a hyperpolarisation-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channel carrying the Ih current that regulates neuronal resting potential, dendritic integration, and rhythmic firing
The phenotype ranges from a Dravet-like developmental and epileptic encephalopathy to milder generalised or febrile seizure syndromes
Seizures often begin in infancy, frequently with fever sensitivity and prolonged or febrile-triggered episodes, mimicking SCN1A-related Dravet syndrome
Multiple seizure types can occur, including focal, generalised tonic-clonic, absence, and myoclonic seizures
Developmental impairment, autistic features, and movement abnormalities may accompany the more severe presentations
Both gain- and loss-of-function variants are described, so the direction of the channel defect can influence excitability and treatment response
Because of the clinical overlap with Dravet syndrome, HCN1 should be considered when SCN1A testing is negative
reference.pathophysiology: HCN1 encodes a subunit of the hyperpolarisation-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channel family responsible for the Ih (or funny) current, which activates on membrane hyperpolarisation and stabilises resting membrane potential while shaping dendritic signal integration and rhythmic oscillations. Pathogenic variants alter channel gating, and both gain- and loss-of-function effects have been reported; either can disturb the fine control of neuronal excitability and dendritic integration. The consequent instability of firing lowers the seizure threshold and, in more severe variants, disrupts developmental circuit maturation, producing the encephalopathic phenotype. Understanding whether a variant increases or decreases Ih helps rationalise antiseizure choices.
additionalDifferentials: SCN1B and GABRG2 related febrile seizure syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Epilepsy gene panel or whole-exome sequencing to identify the HCN1 variant, especially when SCN1A is negative
Electroencephalography to characterise generalised and focal features
Brain magnetic resonance imaging to exclude structural causes
Where feasible, functional characterisation to determine gain versus loss of function
redFlags: Prolonged febrile-triggered seizures or status epilepticus
Emerging movement disorder or severe behavioural deterioration
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the phenotype, with milder febrile and generalised presentations often having favourable cognition, while the Dravet-like encephalopathy carries drug-resistant seizures and intellectual disability.
pitfalls: Anchoring on SCN1A and stopping the workup for a Dravet-like presentation
Assuming a single functional mechanism when both gain and loss of function occur
Underestimating fever sensitivity and the risk of prolonged seizures
Overlooking associated autistic and developmental features
